speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before we commence the debate on the Motion, I wish to draw hon Members' attention to certain provisions in our Standing Orders.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: First of all, Standing Order No 50(1) states that the Member shall confine his observations to the subject under discussion and may not introduce matters irrelevant thereto.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If any Member wishes to widen the debate to discuss general political matters or party issues or the conduct of another Member, he can and he should do so by filing a separate Motion for debate by the House.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Hon Members are to abide by the rules and other provisions of the Standing Orders.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will disallow any remarks which infringe the rules.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are urged to exercise judgement in their speeches and clarifications and to be prepared to substantiate any factual point that they make.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That lie led to another, and another, and yet another, and then to an inquiry by the Committee of Privileges (COP) where more lies were told – this time, under oath.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This resulted in a referral to the Public Prosecutor (PP) and eventually to charges in Court for offences under the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act 1962 (or PPIPA).

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Now, the matter has come full circle back to Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It involves multiple lies to different persons at different times, guiding a junior Member of Parliament (MP) to do the wrong thing and a failure of leadership.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Singapore's Parliamentary democracy, honesty and integrity are not abstract ideals.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The authority of this House does not rest on law alone.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It rests on the confidence and trust that Singaporeans have in Parliament – in its processes and its Members.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is why Parliament must insist that its Members always speak truthfully and act with integrity, even when it is politically inconvenient to do so.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When an MP lies to Parliament or before its committees, it is not just a personal lapse or a tactical misjudgement.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It strikes at the trust Singaporeans place in us as well as the solemn duty we owe to the people we serve.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It undermines the high standards of integrity and incorruptibility which make the Singaporean system work and for which Singapore is known.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is why I have brought this Motion before Parliament today.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Note the findings of the High Court and the COP; 3.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Express regret at Mr Singh's conduct, which was dishonourable and unbecoming of a Member of Parliament; 4.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Note that the High Court's judgment and COP findings have implications for Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Faisal Manap which have to be considered separately; and 6.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Call on all Members of Parliament to uphold our solemn duty to respect and abide by the law, act with integrity at all times and honour the trust placed in us by Singaporeans.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, to be clear, and for avoidance of doubt, in the third limb of the Motion, the one that asks us to express regret, the House is not being asked to impose any penalties or sanctions on Mr Pritam Singh under the PPIPA.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What is being asked is for this House to express a view of his conduct and, if the House agrees that such conduct is not acceptable, to express its regret at such conduct.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Also, the fourth limb of the Motion does not operate to remove the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Leader of the Opposition is designated by the Prime Minister and the decision whether Mr Singh should continue with that designation rests with the Prime Minister, not Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, Members are entitled to and, I would argue, have an obligation to express a view on Mr Singh's suitability to continue in that role.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will then be for the Prime Minister to decide what to do after that.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The fifth limb asks the House to note that the Court judgments have implications for Ms Lim and Mr Faisal, as I will explain in my speech.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, as the extent and degree of their conduct differ from Mr Singh's, the fifth limb proposes that their matters be considered separately on another occasion.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On 3 August 2021, Ms Raeesah Khan, then a Workers' Party (WP) MP, spoke during the WP Motion titled "Empowering Women".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She alleged that three years earlier, she had accompanied a sexual assault survivor to make a police report on a rape committed against the survivor.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She claimed to have witnessed the survivor come out crying and alleged that the police officer commented about the survivor's dressing and the fact that she had been drinking.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Khan repeated this allegation at a later Sitting of Parliament on 4 October 2021.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, on 1 November 2021, she admitted to Parliament that she had lied and had not in fact accompanied a survivor to the police station.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will refer to this lie as the "Untruth" as the Court did.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Following Ms Khan's admission, I raised a complaint against her under Standing Order 100(7)(b) for breach of privilege.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The complaint was referred to the COP, which was convened and began its inquiry on 29 November 2021.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal – then the three senior-most leaders in the WP – gave evidence before the COP to assist in its investigations into the circumstances that led to Ms Khan's Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Khan told the inquiry that the three WP leaders had advised her to continue with the Untruth after she first uttered it in Parliament on 3 August 2021.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, the three WP leaders denied this before the COP.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The COP found each of the three to have lied under oath.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On 15 February 2022, Parliament debated and adopted the COP's Report.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This House fined Ms Khan and resolved to refer Mr Singh to the PP to be investigated for lying to the COP.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh was later charged in Court on 19 March 2024 for lying to a Parliamentary committee, which is an offence under the PPIPA.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Faisal was referred to the PP for refusing to answer the COP's questions.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For this, he was subsequently issued a Police Advisory.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parliament postponed making a decision on: Mr Singh's, Ms Lim's and Mr Faisal's involvement in guiding Ms Khan to continue with the Untruth; and Ms Lim's and Mr Faisal's lying to the COP; pending the outcome of Mr Singh's case.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parliament now has to decide what to do in the light of the Courts' findings.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And that is the reason for the Motion today.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is when it pertains to his conduct in his capacity as an MP and if there is a substantive Motion on the matter.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In this case, we do have a substantive Motion, the terms of which require us to consider the character and conduct of Mr Singh, and at times Ms Lim and Mr Faisal, in light of the High Court judgment and the COP Report, and to make certain decisions after doing so.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is therefore necessary for us not to skirt around the conduct with euphemisms but to name it squarely, so that everyone understands the issues clearly and can debate them properly.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh has stated that he accepts the High Court's judgment "fully and without reservation".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Court findings established many disturbing facts about Mr Singh's conduct.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, he later guided her to continue with the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, he recommended to the WP Central Executive Committee (CEC) that Ms Khan be expelled from WP if she did not resign, but crucially failed to disclose to the CEC his own prior knowledge of Ms Khan's Untruth and his own involvement guiding her to continue with the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Fourth, he lied to Singaporeans when he publicly rejected Ms Khan's accounts of the matter, and accused her of lying.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Fifth, he lied twice to the COP about his own involvement in guiding Ms Khan to maintain her Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Once when he denied telling Ms Khan to take the Untruth to the grave, and again, when he claimed that he had wanted Ms Khan to clarify the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And sixth, Mr Singh stuck to these untruths when giving evidence at trial.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That means he lied to the Courts too.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In gist, this was not a single lapse.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He was also not upfront with his own party.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On 7 August 2021, a few days after Ms Khan told the Untruth in Parliament, she confessed this to Mr Singh over the phone.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The next day, she met him, along with Ms Lim and Mr Faisal.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Khan told them about the Untruth as well.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At this meeting, Mr Singh told Ms Khan to take the Untruth to the grave.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In particular, Ms Khan sent a WhatsApp message to two of her close WP colleagues immediately after the meeting.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The message recorded that the three WP leaders had "agreed that the best thing to do is to take the information to the grave".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Courts also found that at this 8 August meeting, Ms Lim had said that "probably the issue won't come up again", and Mr Singh did not contradict her view.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, before the COP, Mr Singh vehemently denied Ms Khan's account that she had been asked to take the Untruth to the grave.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He said, and I quote, "  would be highly inaccurate.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is a complete lie." The other two WP leaders denied it before the COP too.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All three claimed instead that they did not discuss with Ms Khan what should be done about the Untruth at this 8 August meeting.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh said that she had to speak to her parents first.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh continued to say this during his Court trial.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With the benefit of the Court judgments, we now know that it was in fact Mr Singh and the other two WP leaders who had lied about what was said at this meeting.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Court found that their attitude had been clear and simple: they believed that there was no need to tell the truth because they did not think that the matter would surface again – they thought it would be buried forever.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For the next two months until October 2021, Mr Singh did not discuss the Untruth with Ms Khan, nor do anything to get her to correct it.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was despite him actively monitoring her other Parliamentary work during this time.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On 3 October 2021, one day before Parliament sat on 4 October 2021, Mr Singh visited Ms Khan at her home.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He told Ms Khan he had a feeling that the issue of the Untruth might be raised the next day.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He wanted to discuss what should be done if the topic came up.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The District Court found that during this meeting, Mr Singh guided Ms Khan to continue her Untruth in Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is consistent with the finding of the COP.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, when Mr Singh denied this before the COP and the Court, he was again lying.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The next day, when Minister Shanmugam asked Ms Khan for further details of her anecdote in Parliament, Ms Khan doubled down on the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Both Mr Singh and Ms Lim were present in the House.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When Ms Khan reiterated the Untruth, they did nothing to correct her.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Faisal also learnt about the exchange in Parliament later that day.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The 11 October 2021 meeting with Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Police emailed Ms Khan on 7 October 2021, requesting to interview her to obtain more details for the investigation.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She forwarded this email to Mr Singh and the other two WP leaders.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On 11 October 2021, Mr Singh and Ms Lim consulted Mr Low Thia Khiang, the WP's former Secretary-General, on what steps to take in relation to the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even as they sought Mr Low's advice, they were not honest with him.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Critically, they did not reveal that they had known about Ms Khan's Untruth since 8 August 2021.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Low said he only learned this two years later, in 2023.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At that point, Mr Singh and Ms Lim were also still hopeful that the Government might not discover the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Lim told Mr Low that discovering the Untruth was not easy because "there are so many Police stations in Singapore".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Again, Mr Singh did not disagree with her.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It was Mr Low who impressed upon Mr Singh and Ms Lim that Ms Khan had to clarify the Untruth and apologise to Parliament, regardless of whether it might be discovered by the Government.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was the turning point in the WP's response to the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Following this meeting with Mr Low, arrangements were finally made for Ms Khan to clarify the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She eventually did so via a personal statement in Parliament on 1 November 2021.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In short, Mr Singh and the other two WP leaders hid the truth for months.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They only decided to come clean after Mr Low, their former Secretary-General, advised them to do so.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Disciplinary Panel (DP) proceedings and the press conference.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The day after Ms Khan clarified the Untruth, the WP announced that it had formed a DP to look into her admissions in Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The DP comprised Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal – the very persons to whom she had confessed her Untruth in August 2021, from whom she had sought advice, who had agreed to guide her to take the truth to the grave, and – in the case of Mr Singh – who had said he would not judge her.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Well, he did proceed to sit in judgement upon her, personally.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the course of the DP proceedings, when Ms Khan requested a second interview with the DP, Mr Singh replied: "Dear Raeesah – I hope you can see that it is precisely your character and behaviour that is under review here, in view of your actions in Parliament and your decision to stick to the untruthful anecdote when asked again in October".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What is most troubling about this episode is that Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal failed to declare to the WP CEC or their own party members, let alone the public, that all three of them had actually known about the Untruth since August 2021, and all three had been involved in guiding Ms Khan to maintain her Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One does not need to be a lawyer or a Parliamentarian to know that this is improper and wrong, legally and morally.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As the District Court observed: "there would have been a real concern that the three WP leaders may not be seen to be able to act fairly or impartially when enquiring into Ms Khan's behaviour, as their own conduct in the affair would also come under scrutiny", and they had in fact acted "to conceal their involvement in guiding Ms Khan to maintain the Untruth since 8 August 2021".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh claimed that this information was not provided because it was "irrelevant".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Yet, on 2 December 2021, hours before the COP hearing was due to begin, Mr Singh held a press conference and admitted, for the very first time, that the three WP leaders had known of Ms Khan's Untruth shortly after she had said it on 3 August 2021.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh described this timing as a pure, complete coincidence.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And here is what the District Court found, and I quote: "497.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Before this, even the WP CEC was kept in the dark. 498.   only made his public disclosure after Ms Loh had told Mr Mike Lim to let   know that no matter what happened   would be going into the COP to tell the truth or what   knew of it and   wanted to give   an opportunity to clarify or make a plan where he could put out the party's position or his position first. 499.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In   view,   action in holding the press conference on 2 December 2021 clearly suggested that he was trying to do damage control by pre-emptively disclosing his knowledge and involvement before it was publicly revealed by   Loh or Ms Khan." When Mr Singh appeared before the COP, he continued to lie and to distance himself from Ms Khan's conduct.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He denied making the statement about taking the Untruth to the grave – that was a lie.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He said that he had wanted Ms Khan to tell the truth in October 2021 – that was another lie.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These were even graver than other lies, because he was giving them in evidence before a Parliament committee and he was speaking under oath.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They are findings of the Courts and Mr Singh has said he accepts the Court's judgment fully and without reservation.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, as we can see: Mr Singh guided Ms Khan, twice, to maintain her Untruth to Parliament; he then lied twice before the COP; he lied before the Court; he lied to the public; and he concealed material information from his own party.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, if Mr Singh had told Ms Khan to come clean when she first confessed her Untruth to him in August 2021, the entire matter would have taken a very different course.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Yes, it would have been inconvenient and uncomfortable to disclose the truth then.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The WP had just won their second group representation constituency (GRC) in Sengkang in the 2020 General Election and Ms Khan was a member of WP's Sengkang team.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But the consequences would have been nowhere as grave as what followed Mr Singh's telling Ms Khan to take the Untruth "to the grave".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is precisely at such moments where leaders are tested, and where leadership matters.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And we have seen the contrast between Mr Singh's approach and Mr Low Thia Khiang's leadership.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, there was a failure to take responsibility.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: After Ms Khan told the Untruth, she knew she was in trouble.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She asked Mr Singh for advice, as her party leader and because she regarded him as her mentor.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh told her to hide the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He guided her to continue with the Untruth.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Yet when the truth came to light, he did not admit his complicity.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Instead, he disowned her actions and later sat in judgment of her conduct – while concealing his own role.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, Mr Singh refused to acknowledge the impact of the original Untruth on the Police.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He said no wrong had been done to the Police by reason of the false claim and questioned the amount of work the Police had done to investigate the false claim.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He dismissed the work the Police had to put in and the diversion of public resources with the comment that the Police is not a "broken-back organisation".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This led to delays in handling other matters and cases.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Singh could easily have prevented all this by urging Ms Khan to tell the truth the moment she confessed to him.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Is that not the end of the matter?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are not asking to impose further penalties for those offences or his other misconduct under PPIPA.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But the matters in the Court judgment and the outstanding matters in the COP Report still affect Parliament and Parliament must take a view.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Untruth, which gave rise to the offence, occurred in Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The lies were told to a Committee of Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The conduct and conviction of Mr Singh reflect directly on Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parliament must decide whether such conduct is acceptable for an MP – and in this case the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Following the High Court decision, Mr Singh has not shown any remorse, accountability or acceptance of responsibility.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Nor has the WP expressed its view on the matter.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It has announced some proceedings that are still in progress, but its dilatory response contrasts sharply with its swift actions in previous cases.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the case of Ms Khan, after she confessed her Untruth to Parliament on 1 November 2021, a DP was formed within 24 hours to look into her admission.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Recommendations were made and accepted by the CEC within the month.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the case of Mr Leon Perera, after video evidence of his extra-marital affair emerged on 17 July 2023, Mr Singh met with him that same afternoon and the WP’s CEC met that same evening to discuss the matter.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Two days later, on 19 July 2023, Mr Perera resigned.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It was made known that had he not done so, he would have been expelled.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The WP responded that it was studying the verdict and grounds of decision.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I then issued two statements, on 17 and 22 December, saying that this matter would be raised in Parliament in January.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The DP would conclude within three months and the Special CMC would only be convened after the DP completed its work.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is strange that the WP could act so decisively in the cases of Ms Khan and Mr Perera – where there were no Court findings on their conduct.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Yet now, in a far graver case of dishonesty and lying, it needs four months to figure out the import of the Court's clear judgment of Mr Singh.

speaker: Mr Speaker

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Earlier, you had advised all Members to stick to the matters involved in the resolutions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I wonder, what the Leader has been saying, what has it got to do with the resolutions?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: First, I want to say that indeed, I had made those remarks.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And I had said that we are not questioning the decisions of the Court, but with respect to setting out the context, those can be cited.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I wonder what has that got to do with the resolutions?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the point is what I was getting to, which is that, while I understand that this is what the WP is doing, Parliament cannot wait on the WP nor should our view depend on the WP's internal deliberations —

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Maybe I should explain to him step by step.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If a statement is made to the Court and the Court finds that that is not true or rejects it, it must follow, as a matter of logic, that what was told to the Court, is not the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Court can decide whether or not it wishes to proceed with perjury, but the Court does not have to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The point I am making is that: what was told to the Court, if untrue, it must follow that it is a lie.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If I may be permitted to continue, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I was saying, Parliament cannot wait on the WP nor should our view depend on the WP's internal deliberations, or on whether Mr Singh's actions contravene the WP constitution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This House must decide on the matter without unnecessary delay, as it reflects on the standing and integrity of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh was first designated the Leader of the Opposition by then Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong after the 2020 General Election.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: After the 2025 General Election, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong again designated Mr Singh as the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The office of the Leader of the Opposition was formally established in 2020 to recognise Singaporeans' strong desire for a greater diversity of views in our politics and to enable our political system to evolve in a way that maintains our sense of national purpose.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He has greater responsibilities and privileges than other backbenchers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To recap, the duties of the Leader of the Opposition include leading the Opposition in presenting alternative views in Parliamentary debates on policies, Bills and Motions; scrutinising the Government's positions and actions in Parliament; and nominating opposition Members for appointment to Select Committees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, the Leader of the Opposition may be asked to take on other duties, such as attending official state functions, and taking part in visits and meetings alongside members of the Government and the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When he does so, he goes as a representative of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Leader of the Opposition also receives specific privileges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He will, from time to time, receive confidential briefings by the Government on important national issues, such as security and external relations, especially during a national crisis or emergency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In debates, he gets the right of first response and more time for his speeches, equal to a Minister's speech time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He is provided an office in Parliament; additional staff support and resources and double the allowance of an elected MP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Clearly, the Leader of the Opposition position carries important duties and privileges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Whoever holds this designation must be respected and trusted as a competent representative of the people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The WP MPs have often made speeches in this House about the importance of accountability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have declared it their mission to hold the Government to account.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The question is whether they believe that their own members – including their leader – should also be held to account for doing something wrong, especially after the Court has convicted them of a crime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The WP and Mr Singh himself have expressed strong views against lying and dishonesty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: After Ms Khan lied to Parliament and after the cover-up failed, Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal recommended to the WP CEC that she be expelled from the party if she did not resign.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When Mr Leon Perera was discovered to have lied to the WP leadership about his extramarital affair, Mr Singh said, "The Constitution of the Workers' Party requires candidates to be honest and frank in their dealings with the party and the people of Singapore… Leon's conduct and not being truthful when asked by the party leadership about the allegation fell short of the standards expected of WP MPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Had he not offered his resignation, I would have recommended to the CEC that he be expelled from the party." Notably, swift justice was meted out just for lying to the WP leadership.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Khan and Mr Perera had not lied to a Committee of Parliament or under oath; and Mr Perera had not been charged for a crime, let alone found guilty by the Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am sure the WP will agree with me that the same standards and rigour must apply, whether to backbenchers or party leaders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Of course, the same standards apply also to People's Action Party (PAP) MPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If a PAP MP or Political Office Holder is found guilty of lying or dishonesty, nobody doubts that serious consequences will follow.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would be untenable for them to continue as if nothing happened.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In serious cases, they will have to relinquish their positions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Members may recall that in 1999, PAP MP Choo Wee Khiang was charged for cheating.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In 2024, Mr S Iswaran resigned as soon as he was charged, even before conviction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin resigned on account of his personal conduct, even though there was no criminal offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These standards underpin our system of Government and are crucial to providing Singaporeans with the quality of leaders and Government that they deserve.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They form the foundation of our political system and of good governance in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The damage would be profound and exceedingly difficult to recover from.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I therefore ask all Members to support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The Leader of the House characterised it as a cover-up.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: That was not found in the Court filings.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: So, under Standing Order 50(6), I do not believe that is permissible.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The Leader of the House characterised it as a cover-up, which was not found in the legal judgment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: So, I do not believe this is permissible under Standing Order 50(6), which involves imputing improper motives.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One moment, Mr Speaker, so that I can be very clear.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Tiong has just raised a Point of Order.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He says that the Court did not use the word or did not find there was a cover-up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are free to vote as they consider fit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On my submissions and response to what the Leader has said, including going through aspects of the judgment, my submissions to the Court and my defence are found online.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have posted all my defence submissions online.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is no further right of appeal to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One has to accept the verdict fully and without reservation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will explain why I was disappointed with the judgment, a public comment which I did not hear from the Leader's opening.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will explain why I was disappointed with the judgment and therefore do not agree with it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I will make some general points first and address all the resolutions of the Motion in the course of my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will use the word "resolutions" in my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The defence's position, amongst other things, was straightforward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Courts have ruled that her SMS message of 8 August of having been told to take her lie to the grave was the anchoring piece of documentary evidence and, along with other circumstantial evidence, led to the trial judge's conclusion that such a statement was made by myself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As for the other circumstantial evidence used to sustain my conviction, the legal opinion of the defence at trial was that enough evidence was canvassed to Court to render a conviction on both charges, unsafe in law, with reasonable doubt, duly established.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This explains why the defence's considered view was that there was no necessity for me to call Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Faisal Manap up as witnesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is all I will say on this point, in concert with Speaker's earlier ruling, as I do not intend to use my speech to review matters the Court has deliberated and ruled upon.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, the law has run its course – and I accept and respect that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On Resolution 1 of the Motion, as an Opposition MP, my colleagues and I play a role in upholding our Organs of State.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This disposition explains why I have no difficulty agreeing with Resolution 1 of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On Resolution 2, it is worthwhile to recall that the COP's findings went much further than the charges that were preferred against me.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a fact that the subject of guiding Khan to continue to lie, which is found in the Leader of the House's Motion, was not framed as a charge that was preferred against me.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Parliament would recall that it had referred my matter to the Police and the PP to review all evidence afresh.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It follows that the PP would have no trouble framing a charge to this effect if indeed there was sufficient evidence that I had guided Khan to lie.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My position is Khan was not told to lie, let alone guided to lie.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, Sir, let me refer to some reports that were published in The Straits Times as the appeal was heard: "3.40 pm, 4 November last year – Justice Chong says the Prosecution's point that Mr Singh did not stand up to clarify on 4 October 2021 when Ms Khan doubled down on her lie in Parliament is not remarkable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is not realistic to expect him to immediately react to what she said was a lie, he says.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This can cut both ways as events subsequently demonstrate, he adds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Judge notes that it is unrealistic to say that just because Singh did not stand up that day to clarify, it does not mean that doubling down is something he told her to do." I also refer to the notes of evidence of 4 November on appeal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Court to my lawyer: "But you are pitching your case to say that Mr Singh never told her to lie, but that might be right." My lawyer: "I am not pitching it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I mean, factually, as Your Honour has recognised, that is right.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Owing to relatively recent developments to the criminal law, the prosecution today must hand over witness statements in its possession that are favourable to my case before the trial begins.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a legal obligation under what I refer to as the Kadar disclosure rules.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As per law, I was given portions of Loh Pei Ying's statements that she made to the Police.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, such statements are inadmissible in court, subject to the criteria in section 259 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and subject to the usual rules of evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, under section 225A of the Criminal Procedure Code, permission must be given by the PP to use the undisclosed statements outside trial proceedings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, Parliament is sovereign, which means it is supreme above all other Government institutions, including the executive and judicial bodies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And for Parliamentary purposes, Police statements under oath must be official documents and the reply to one question goes to the heart of my position in rejecting Resolution 3 of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Members would remember that these Police statements arose out of Parliament's referral of Mr Faisal and myself to the PP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As Parliament is sovereign, I would like to pass up a copy to Speaker for his consideration before permission is given to me to read out one question and its corresponding answer.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Singh, you may hand the document over to the Clerk.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The statements that Mr Singh is referring to, is he referring to statements that the PP had provided him for purposes of the trial?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And Mr Singh's answer was, "That is correct".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And Mr Singh's position was that he had asked — So, that was provided during the trial?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, Mr Singh is now asking, or he says that he had asked the PP for permission to use them for today's Motion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And Mr Singh is asking Mr Speaker to rule to allow the Prosecution's statement for this Motion?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And Mr Singh is asking the Speaker to rule —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: What you have provided to me, Mr Singh, is something which you had stated the PP or rather the Police have refused to release to you.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The statement that I have handed over to Speaker was not admissible in Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it remains a Police statement made under oath and my application, if I can call it that, is to allow me to recite the question and answer to that statement, because it is of relevance to Resolution 3 in the Motion.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have not looked at the provisions myself, but perhaps Mr Singh can clarify.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has asked the Attorney-General's Chamber (AGC), and AGC has said no.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Is there a legal provision that governs the use of such documents and does that give AGC the power to say yes or no?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, perhaps I can read out from that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And the answer would be in the affirmative.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But because I have the provision, let me just read it out. "Restrictions on use of materials disclosed by the prosecution, section 225A.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: (1) Where the prosecution discloses (whether before, on or after 17 September 2018) any material to the accused or the accused’s advocate (if any) for the purposes of any criminal proceedings — (a) that material may be disclosed, for the purposes of those criminal proceedings, to any co‑accused in those criminal proceedings, or to the advocate (if any) of any such co‑accused, by any of the following persons: (i) the accused; (ii) the accused’s advocate (if any); (iii) any other co‑accused or advocate to whom that material was disclosed under this paragraph.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: (b) on and after 17 September 2018, each of the following persons is deemed to give an undertaking to the court not to use that material for any purpose (other than the purposes of those criminal proceedings) without the permission of the Public Prosecutor".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is as I thought, Sir, I have not read it recently, but as a point of clarification, and I am sure Speaker can get advice, but it would appear that it is set out in a legislative provision that such information can only be released within the framework set out in that legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And maybe, I am not sure that I have ever come across a situation where Parliament can ignore the legal position set out in law.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will make a ruling on this later.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There are those who believe that whatever our Courts decide, a convicted person is unable to retain their belief that they are innocent insofar as a conviction is concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In 1994, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam was convicted for a different criminal offence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The President, who opened this very session of Parliament only some months back, was asked about this in an interview with the online news channel, Mothership, just prior to his election victory in the 2023 Presidential Elections.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He said in response to his conviction that, I quote, "They got the wrong man." A criminal conviction does not negate one's right to assert innocence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A finding of guilt by the Courts did not undermine the President's personal view of his conviction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In fact, this was not the first time that I had taken responsibility to this effect.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I had done so in similar terms publicly three times before: first at the COP itself, next at the debate on the COP Report and finally, at the trial Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I did not have close to three years to deal with a sensitive matter involving one of my MPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That said, I reiterate, I should have done better in balancing the need to be sensitive to Khan for the reason she gave for lying to Parliament on the one hand and resolving the matter of a lie in Parliament as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Resolution 4 asserts that my continuation in the Leader of the Opposition role would undermine public confidence in the integrity of Singapore's political system, amongst other things.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the matter of the Leader of the Opposition appointment, I refer to a question that was asked of me by Daryl Lim, a Lianhe Zaobao reporter, on 4 May 2025, one day after Polling Day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He asked, "In the next Parliament, it looks like the PAP and the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As Leader of the Opposition, what does it look like for the future of the opposition in Singapore?" I answered, "I don't know whether I'm going to be Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is something the government of the day has to decide.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, let's see what happens there." In Singapore, the Leader of the Opposition appointment is not a constitutional or statutory one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have never operated on the assumption that the Leader of the Opposition appointment is a given, nor have I hankered for it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the course of her speech, Leader of the House made a tangential point about the other duties of the Leader of the Opposition, including following Government on overseas trips and receiving classified briefings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Perhaps, for good order, the Leader can share how many of such briefings were extended to me and how many trips I went with the Government to various places for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, my colleagues and I see a better future for Singapore and Singaporeans, with a more balanced Parliament and a democratic society based on justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The future we envisage for Singapore does not call for the destruction of the stable and sensible politics Singaporeans seek to uphold in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that makes Resolution 6 of the Motion unobjectionable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In fact, my predecessor, Mr Low Thia Khiang, after giving evidence at my trial, said to the media, I quote: "The voters can make a distinction between who is a good politician and who is not a good politician, and I believe Pritam Singh is a good politician.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He is a capable, competent leader with a heart for Singapore and Singaporeans." To be clear, I do not undertake my political work for such testimonies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am grateful for the support of Singapore and Singaporeans, and like my colleagues and leaders before me, all of us endeavour to do our best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In my case, whatever Parliament decides and as long as I am an MP, I will continue my work as a MP on the ground in Aljunied GRC, and I will continue to advocate for Singaporeans in Parliament to the best of my abilities, as I have for the last 15 years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For the WP and to my fellow Singaporeans, we press on and we continue working for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Does anyone wish to speak on this Motion?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I do not personally know the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This being only my third day in Parliament, I have so far not had the opportunity to meet Mr Pritam Singh and make his acquaintance.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: My profession – the legal profession – is an honourable one, and its members are held to high ethical standards to act with integrity and honesty, to uphold justice and to preserve the public's trust.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I am one of the Senior Counsel who sit on the Panel of Disciplinary Tribunal Presidents on the Law Society of Singapore disciplinary cases.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This means that when a complaint is made against a practising lawyer alleging professional misconduct and the matter is deemed serious enough to warrant investigation by a Disciplinary Tribunal, I have from time to time been appointed to preside over such cases.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: In considering these cases, the Disciplinary Tribunal must first be satisfied that the charges of professional misconduct are proven beyond reasonable doubt.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The Tribunal must then consider if due cause has been shown that would warrant referring the lawyer to the Court of Three Judges, for consideration of disciplinary action.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Just to explain to Members that findings that would justify such a referral for disciplinary action include cases where the advocate and solicitor: one, has been convicted of a criminal offence, implying a defect of character which makes him or her unfit for the profession; two, has been found guilty of fraudulent or grossly improper conduct in the discharge of his or her professional duty, or guilty of certain breaches that amount to improper conduct or practice as an advocate and solicitor; and three, has been guilty of misconduct unbefitting an advocate and solicitor as an officer of the Supreme Court or as a member of an honourable profession.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: That list is not intended to be exhaustive.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I should also mention that as legal counsel, I advise the medical profession, which is another profession that is held to high standards of ethical conduct.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Doctors, dentists, nurses and allied health professionals are also subjected to self-regulation in the form of a complaints and disciplinary process.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: If allegations of professional misconduct are proven and due cause is shown, a doctor's privileges to practice could be suspended or revoked.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: And like lawyers, doctors can be disciplined by their own professional body, even if the doctor has already been separately held accountable in a Court of law and convicted for a criminal offence.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: One is accountable to the law, in a criminal Court, but must also be accountable to one's own profession.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, the professions of law and medicine have much in common.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: In July 2017, the Honourable the Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon delivered the 23rd Gordon Arthur Ransome Oration entitled, “Law and Medicine: Professions of Honour, Service and Excellence”, in which he referenced lawyers and doctors as the “sibling professions of law and medicine”, who serve critical functions in contemporary society.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: He called on members of both professions to, among other things, “appreciate and commit to their shared calling to public service”, and “to serve with excellence in ethics as well as competence, so as not to betray the trust of the laypersons who rely on professionals to safeguard their interests and welfare”.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: In another important speech he would go on to deliver in March 2018 entitled, “Medicine and Law: Comparative Perspectives on Professional Conduct and Discipline”, our Chief Justice will go on to say, and again, I quote, "It is for the sake of the protection of the public, therefore, that the professions have always sought to regulate themselves and to punish those of their number who are guilty of misconduct.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The special privileges that we receive as lawyers and doctors can be taken away, if we do not live up to the standards of honesty and probity that is expected from us.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: What more, if one is an MP in service of the public?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: What more, if one is the Leader of the Opposition, who has been specially conferred with the privileges and respect that comes with that special position?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: And what the Chief Justice has alluded to about professional bodies always seeking to regulate themselves and having processes to enforce standards is, to me, what this Motion is all about.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It is not enough for any profession to simply claim to have standards of conduct and declare itself an honourable profession.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Upholding the rule of law means we must accept the finality and authority of our Court judgments.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The District Judge rendered his decision only after weighing all the evidence, hearing the parties’ submissions and applying the law without fear or favour.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: His decision was in turn scrutinised closely by a very senior appellate judge, who was satisfied that the conviction must be upheld.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Whether we like the outcome or find it disappointing, the integrity of our legal system depends on our commitment to honour the result.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: And I am glad that following the unsuccessful appeal, Mr Pritam Singh had publicly stated that he accepts the Court’s judgment fully and without reservation, although it now seems that he has clarified he accepts the Court’s decision only because there is no other avenue of appeal, not because he actually agrees that the decision was correct.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: To wilfully give false answers must mean that the conduct leading to conviction involved dishonesty.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The first paragraph of the Motion asks that we affirm that honesty and integrity are fundamental pillars of Singapore’s parliamentary and political system.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: To this, I say that there should be no question in the minds of any reasonable right-thinking person, that that must be the case.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: If the public that we serve are to have trust and confidence in our systems, they have every right to demand that honesty and integrity be the fundamental pillars by which we conduct ourselves and Parliament’s business, and there should be no hesitation on our part to support paragraph 1 of the Motion, as well as paragraph 6 of the Motion, which calls upon all MPs to uphold their solemn duty to respect and abide by the law, act with integrity at all times and honour the trust placed in them by Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I would go so far as to say that if we were to vote on each paragraph of the Motion separately, if anyone were to vote “no” to paragraph 1 and paragraph 6, that would automatically raise serious questions about their fitness to serve.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: As I have explained, the need to characterise misconduct and consider if it is serious enough to potentially warrant the curtailment or stripping away of certain special privileges is certainly not a decision that is new to me, when I preside over a Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: What I can say is this – when we make our deliberations and vote on the Motion, it must never be based on personal factors but purely on the objective standards of conduct that we are called to uphold and in circumstances where an authoritative finding of guilt has already been made.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I trust that all of us will approach the Motion in the same way and make our judgment based on these unassailable principles and sound objective considerations.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We are all human and we all make mistakes.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We may commit errors of judgement, maybe even serious ones.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The true test of our character lies not in our failings or what we may have done on our worst day.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It is in how we respond, whether we are able to openly acknowledge our wrongdoings, show genuine remorse and contrition, not seeking to lay blame elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It would be the clearest sign he could offer this House that he has indeed learned the error of his ways, and he acknowledges that the trust and respect that comes with the position of Leader of the Opposition is one that he now has to work hard to earn back.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, as the saying goes, "To err is human." But there is also an adage that states, "To recognise one's mistakes and to correct them is a great virtue." Indeed, everyone makes mistakes in life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Learning from those mistakes is part of growth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, making mistakes is not to be feared; what truly matters is how we respond to and handle those mistakes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today's Motion, unfortunately, arose because of MPs who repeatedly mishandled their error in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: MPs carry the trust and mandate of the people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Here, we debate and legislate on international issues, governance policies and issues affecting the livelihoods of citizens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This is not only about the future of our nation, it directly impacts the lives of our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Moreover, the quality of our Parliament not only reflects our democracy and governance capabilities but also embodies the values and aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: When the international community observes our Parliament, they do not only focus on the legislative process and policy formulation; they are also assessing Singapore's performance as a modern nation in terms of our integrity and transparency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This responsibility falls not just on the Cabinet but also on all MPs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, a high-quality Parliament can enhance Singapore's image on the global stage, strengthening the trust and willingness of other countries to cooperate with us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: MPs being responsible in Parliament is therefore also being responsible to Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Under the leadership of several generations of leaders and through the collective efforts of our people, Singapore has overcome numerous challenges, rising from a third world country to a first world nation today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As Singapore develops, the needs of our people have become increasingly diverse, and the challenges we face have grown more complex.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In this context, we must ensure that our Parliament is inclusive and adaptive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: While diverse voices and opinions are welcomed, there must be a shared consensus: our Parliament must uphold and demonstrate the principles of honesty, integrity, and accountability, thereby maintaining its credibility and ensuring its effective operation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Many of you may be familiar with the Chinese proverb, "Three men make a tiger," which originated from the "Strategies of the Warring States." In ancient times, before Pang Gong was sent to country Zhao, he told the King of Wei, "If someone in the market says there is a tiger, you won't believe it; if two people say it, you will begin to doubt; if three people say it, you will believe it." Thus, a lie that is repeated three times will become indistinguishable from the truth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, when the first lie is discovered, it must be stopped to prevent a second or even a third from occurring.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Otherwise, this illusion of truth can mislead the public, which is extremely dangerous.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Once a crack is formed, the hole will only grow larger.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We may hold differing opinions and debate them, but this must be based on facts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Given that Parliament is the pillar of our democratic system and the significant role of the Leader of the Opposition, we now face a situation that is deeply disappointing and saddening.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Our Parliament has witnessed several outstanding, responsible and respected Opposition leaders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Mr Low championed honesty, transparency and accountability in his leadership of the WP, something that many have witnessed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We must reach a conclusion and move forward as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: There are still issues regarding the livelihoods of the people and of national imperative that we must address, so we need to redirect the attention and energy of Parliament back to these crucial matters.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I did not come into Parliament to speak on matters of political conduct or party leadership.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: My instinct and my focus, as an NMP, has always been on the practical challenges facing our economy – on business competitiveness, jobs, costs and how Singapore continues to thrive in an increasingly uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I want to state clearly at the outset: I have respect for the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: From my study of his speeches and my limited personal interactions, I believe that his heart, like that of many Members in this House, is for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Differing views, even strong disagreement, are not a weakness in a political system.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: They are often a source of renewal, correction and long-term resilience.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: What we have and what we have always relied upon is trust.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Trust that truth matters, especially when it is uncomfortable.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the apex of these institutions stands Parliament.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The historian Arnold Toynbee, in his extensive study of civilisations, observed that civilisations rarely collapse because of external attack; they collapse because of internal failure.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As he put it succinctly, "Civilizations die from suicide, not by murder." This lesson is sobering.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Nations unravel not when they face challenges, but when their core institutions fail to respond with honesty, discipline and moral clarity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When standards are bent, when truth becomes negotiable, truth erodes quietly at first, and then decisively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As former NMP Ms Janet Ang, once observed in this House, institutional credibility is hard won but easily lost, and once lost, extremely difficult to restore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In a small, open economy like Singapore, trust is not just a moral value – it is a strategic asset.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: From the perspective of business and investment, this is not theoretical.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Investors assess not only tax regimes or incentives, but whether a country's institutions are reliable, predictable and principled.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Investors and businesses price in uncertainty and growth slows.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This reinforces a simple reality: trust is not an abstract ideal.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's attractiveness as an investment hub, and as a hub for trade and innovation, rests on the confidence that our institutions are fair, reliable and accountable.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is because of this centrality of trust that I feel compelled to speak today, even though this matter lies outside my usual substantive terrain.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, Mr Speaker, I approach this Motion with care.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This debate arises from a matter that has been tested through due process and adjudicated by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As my fellow former NMP, Mr Raj Joshua Thomas, has observed in past debates, truthfulness is not a mere procedural requirement; it is what gives legitimacy to our laws and moral authority to our decisions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, Mr Speaker, I reflected on a simple litmus test – not as a lawyer, but drawing on leadership experience, institutional stewardship and my role as an NMP.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We serve without party affiliation and without an electoral mandate.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our legitimacy rests entirely on the trust and confidence of those who appointed us, and of this House.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If an NMP were to lie to Parliament, be tried in a Court of law, and be convicted, the first question he or she must confront is not a legal one, but an institutional one: do I still hold the trust and confidence of those who appointed me?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the answer, in such circumstances, would almost invariably be "no".

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The proper course would be to step aside from any position of responsibility within this House – not as a matter of punishment, but as a matter of integrity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That duty is amplified when the offence itself is dishonesty directed at the very institution one serves.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Trust cannot be compartmentalised; it is either present, or it is not.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Applying that same standard consistently, I find it difficult to argue that lesser expectations should apply where the office in question is a Parliamentarian leadership position, carrying defined responsibilities, duties and privileges.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is, of course, a matter of judgement.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And I state my judgement unreservedly as an NMP, exercising the responsibility entrusted to me by this House – to bring an independent, non-partisan perspective grounded in the national interest.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That moment reminded me that what we do in this House must stand not only for today, but for the next generation of Singaporeans who will inherit these institutions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Speaker, in mid-December, media reports quoted the Leader of the House announcing that Parliament would be discussing what should follow after the High Court judgment in Mr Pritam Singh's case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I was waiting to see what resolutions the Leader would ask Parliament to pass.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: After three weeks of anticipation, the Motion we are debating today is entitled "Expression of Regret at the Conduct of Mr Pritam Singh and Consideration of his Suitability to Continue as Leader of the Opposition." Sir, I wish to offer my personal views on some of the key resolutions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: As I am an interested party in the matter, I stress that these views are my own and I am not speaking for the WP in this regard.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, on Resolutions 2 to 4, touching on Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: After a trial, Mr Singh was convicted and his appeal was dismissed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It bears highlighting the differences between the present case involving Mr Singh and previous instances, when MPs have misconduct themselves and had resigned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Mr Singh's case is unlike the other instances where the MPs themselves admitted their wrongdoings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Mr Singh has maintained his innocence, contested the charges and appealed against his conviction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Court has, however, found him guilty and his conviction has been upheld on appeal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Given the different circumstances of Mr Singh, the question that arises is whether Parliament should subject Mr Singh to a further punishment, by initiating a removal of him from his position as the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Indeed, when Parliament reopened last September, I spoke about the importance of Parliament as an institution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I pointed out that under the World Justice Project's Rule of Law Index rankings, the Singapore Parliament was not faring well in its fundamental task of being an effective check on the Executive Government's powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I urged that all of us in this House see each other as fellow Singaporeans who are not enemies, but competitors who had common cause in serving fellow citizens through this House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I emphasised our duty to ensure that this House served the interests of citizens outside the House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is unhealthy and not in the national interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I must disagree with a linkage between the High Court judgment and my position.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Earlier in statements to the media, the Leader of the House had stated that the COP had found that Mr Singh, Mr Faisal and I had lied to the Committee by denying that we had told Ms Raeesah Khan to hide her Untruth in an August 2021 meeting.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Leader then asserted that, and I quote, "the COP's findings have been borne out by the Court's judgments." Sir, Mr Singh was prosecuted and convicted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: On appeal, the Court upheld Mr Singh's conviction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Neither Mr Faisal nor I participated in the trial.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I was interviewed by the Police several times in late 2022 and so was Mr Faisal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: My impression was that I might be called as a prosecution witness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Following my interviews with the Police and the submission of my written statement to them, I was not called as a witness by the Prosecution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The COP in its conclusions had noted that I had voluntarily tended evidence that was damaging to Mr Singh.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I had spoken about this matter in Parliament on 15 February 2022, when I had explained that the COP had omitted to refer to parts of my evidence given at the COP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I had said that my evidence, if considered as a whole, would not support the COP's conclusions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: That was roughly eight months before I was interviewed by the Police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Court's findings cannot be held against us.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Leader, a Senior Counsel with decades of litigation experience, will no doubt be aware of what I had just said.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Parliament had already decided to refer Mr Singh and Mr Faisal to the PP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The matter was, no doubt, fully and thoroughly investigated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Mr Singh was prosecuted and eventually convicted, while the Prosecution decided not to charge Mr Faisal, but to issue him with an Advisory.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The advisory was to advise Mr Faisal to familiarise himself with the conduct expected of MPs under PPIPA and advising him to refrain from any act that may be in breach of it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Thus, the referral to the PP had reached its conclusion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I state once again that I disagree with the COP's conclusions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Resolution 5 states that the matters regarding Mr Faisal and myself have to be considered separately.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I must say that this is very vague.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Would the Leader be so kind as to elaborate on what is meant and how long we will need to wait for this to be addressed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: If Parliament wishes to take any further steps against me and Mr Faisal, would we be given an opportunity to address Parliament before it proceeds to do so?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We have received emails and letters of encouragement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Many Singaporeans have also approached us individually in hawker centres and malls to voice their concerns over this debate.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It comes at a time when many Singaporeans are highlighting pressing issues that have a direct impact on their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are also navigating the most challenging geopolitical landscape in recent memory.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Be that as it may, the Motion is before us and it is our duty as Parliamentarians to treat it with the utmost seriousness.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
